Having seen and experienced all [other methods] among elixirs, [one realizes that this] is the most essential, the most excellent, and the easiest for men to accomplish: the Great Hero, whose every desire is fulfilled, becomes composed of eternal bliss. (220)
The applications of medicinal pills for strengthening the body have been described; they bring about supreme auspiciousness and lead to constant, excellent success.
Thus ends the third instruction, titled "The Alchemy of Pills," in the section on *rasāyana* within the *Rasaratnākara* composed by the Siddha Śrī Nityanātha, son of Pārvatī.

Now begins the fourth instruction: Lead, mercury, sulphur, iron, and copper, when processed and turned into the supreme nectar, as well as even a single desired group of medicinal roots, when consumed, quickly bring about the perfection of the body.
The great elixir beginning with *kānta* and others consists of dead *kānta*, mica, mercury, sulphur, *mṛṅga*, *viḍaṅga*,
and the seeds of *bilva* (excluding the bark), sixteen *palas* of each. (2)
One should mix thirty palas of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), thirty palas each of ghee and honey, ten palas of citramūla, and all [the remaining ingredients] as a powder.
Then, one should add three palas of triphalā and four hundred [palas] of the aforementioned [base].
One should boil [the ingredients] with eight times their weight of water until one-eighth remains;
this decoction should be used to saturate the previously prepared powder for one month.
One should always drink half a *pala* of that [mixture] from an iron vessel in the hot sun.
If one takes it with milk at the time of sleep for a year, it removes death and old age;
the child [of such a practice] will have firm joints and live as long as the moon, sun, and stars.
This is a divine great elixir (mahārasāyana) that satisfies hundreds of women.
Regarding the mercurial formulations involving mica:
one should cast black mica, heated by fire until it glows like fire, into milk;
then, having split its layers, one should immerse it in water.
One should carefully add thirty palas of black pepper and five palas of powdered [substance] to it; at the end of three days,
one should remove all of that, grind it finely, and bind it with a white cloth.

One should place [the substance] in a jar filled with water within a *gharma* vessel using a *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus). When the water has dried, one should add more water until it has reached the [substance].
Then, one should discard that *abhra* (mica) and the cloth, but preserve the water.
Then the wise man should divide that water containing the mica into thirty parts;
having stirred it with one part of that, he should add one *pala* of white rice and cook it in thirty *palas* of cow’s milk until it has cooled.

The practitioner should daily consume [this preparation] combined with two *pala* each of honey and clarified butter, and one *niṣka* each of black pepper; after a month, it removes death and old age.
Indeed, his hair, teeth, and nails fall out and grow back again.
One shall become a perfected being with a vajra-body, possessing the speed of the wind and great strength.
This is the *amṛtābhra* (nectar-cloud) yoga, proclaimed of old by Śambhu:
take equal parts of purified *mṛtābhra* (dead-iron), pure sulphur, and long pepper, along with clarified butter.
One should eat one *karṣa* daily; after a year, it removes death and old age.
Take equal parts of *koraṇṭaka* leaves, mercury, mica, and sulfur;
all of this should be processed with the juices of *nīlikā* for seven days in the sun.
One should drink one *karṣa* of that with milk for a year; it removes death and old age.
Likewise, having ground one *karṣa* of processed mica (*mṛtābhra*), one *pala* of cow's milk, fresh *sarpākṣī* along with its roots and leaves, and sulfur, [one should consume it].
Having combined them all, one should drink the entire mixture; in one year, one shall conquer old age, possess a vajra-body, become a sky-walker (khecara), and live for three days of Brahmā.
[One should take] mercury, mica, magnetite, and triphalā, along with an equal amount of māgadhī.
One should administer five parts of *badarī* powder mixed with an equal amount of mica (*abhra*).
Combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter, one should always consume half a *pala* of this;
it destroys old age and death within a year, and one's lifespan shall become as long as a day of Brahmā.
"O Amṛtakrīḍā, O Concealer of Viṣṇu, svāhā!
By means of this mantra, all iron-based compounds (*abhraka-yoga*) should be consecrated and consumed;
[this is] the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
Moistened with mercury,
they are drawn [together]; these are the elixirs of mercury through the application of iron.
One should prepare equal quantities of black sesame seeds, powdered jujube fruit, and powdered *kākatuṇḍī* seeds from a deceased beloved;
these should then be processed with the juices of *śālmalī* and *mallikā* leaves for three days.
Having impregnated it for three days with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should dry it again.
Then, having added an equal amount of jaggery (*guḍa*) to that, one should make pills weighing one *karṣa* each.
One should always drink them with the juice extracted from *rudantī*, or with milk, honey, and clarified butter (*ājya*).
In one year, it destroys old age and death; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
One should powder black sesame seeds, *triphalā*, and the deceased beloved in equal parts, and stir them with the juices of *śālmalī* and *ketakī* in a vessel made of the beloved’s bone.
One should drink half a pala of this, which has been kept overnight, in the morning; it destroys death.
By doing so for one year, it overcomes old age, and one may live for three days of Brahmā.
[One should also use] the ash of *kāntaloha*, powdered *kaṇā* (long pepper), and the exudate of *nimba*.
One should lick a half-pala of equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with honey and ghee daily for eight months; such a person shall live for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Having boiled pieces of kuṣṭha in an equal quantity of the decoction of the three myrobalans, [one should proceed as follows].
Having dried and then powdered those [ingredients], one should take an equal amount of *kānta* iron and its calcined ash;
by licking a *karṣa* of this with honey and clarified butter for a year, one destroys death and old age.
Furthermore, the powder of *koraṇṭa* leaves, *kānta* ash, sesame seeds, and jaggery [may be used].
Half a pala of that [mercury] is an equal amount of edible [substance]; by consuming it for a year, death and old age are removed.
One should daily lick four niṣkas of the powder of *kāntaloha* mixed with an equal amount of sulphur and oils derived from *jyotiṣmatī*; thus a man attains the lifespan of Brahmā.
Within a year, he will certainly become equal to Bṛhaspati in speech.
Three parts of mercury (mṛtatīkṣṇa) and eight parts of pure sulfur should be processed for twenty-one days in the heat with the juices of the kanyā plant.
One should drink one karṣa of that with cow's milk; one will live for three days of Brahmā (a kalpa), and after only one year, there is no doubt, one will possess divine luster and great strength.
One should lick equal parts of dead iron, magnetite, and pure mica, along with honey and clarified butter.
One should live for three days of Brahmā (one thousand years) by consuming one niṣka each year.
Alternatively, one should drink three niṣkas of either *mṛtatīkṣṇa*, *muṇḍa*, or *kānta* with warm milk; this arrests the aging of men.
By practicing this for two years, one may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Having thoroughly smeared one *pala* of *dhātrī* powder with auspicious water (*śivāmbu*) onto a vessel made of *kānta* [metal],
one should consume it after rising in the morning.
Freed from wrinkles and graying hair, one shall conquer death within a year.
One should smear one *pala* of *triphalā* and honey inside a vessel of *kānta* iron;
after it has stood for a day and night, it should be drunk daily with the water of *śivā*.
Within a year, it destroys death and old age; one shall live for three hundred years.

*Oṃ haḥ amṛte amṛtaśakti amṛtagandhopajīvi niṣpannaṃ candrāmṛtaṃ ājñāpitaṃ kuru kuru svāhā he he haṃ haḥ gam*. This is the mantra for consuming sulfur and metals; after all metal preparations, there should be the drinking of milk.
One should taste the sweet fresh juice of musta grass, pressed with the teeth;
one should eat its roots to alleviate a bad taste in the mouth.
When the digestive tract is bound and the digestive fire is blazing, one should always drink warm milk.
When constipation occurs, one should avoid bathing, massage, pungent substances, and hot foods;
however, one should constantly and repeatedly chew betel leaf with camphor.
Once the food is properly digested and the digestive fire is stimulated, one may drink [liquids] when hungry.
Boiled milk and then food should be consumed during the iron-elixir therapy.
[Now begins] the Brahmavṛkṣa Kalpa:
the five parts of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, dried in the shade and finely powdered.
One should lick a karṣa measure of this with honey and clarified butter; in one year, one shall conquer old age.
Possessing divine luster and great strength, one shall live for a thousand years.
One should cause the flowers of the Brahma-tree (Brahmavṛkṣa) to be dried in the shade.
Having combined thirty palas of that powder with twenty-four palas of ghee, one should place them in a vessel, seal it, and bury it in a heap of grain.
After one month, having extracted it, one should divide it into fourteen portions.
By practicing this for three years, one should daily consume one-sixtieth part [of the substance] from a beautiful vessel;
if one acts thus for three months, that person shall possess a vajra-body.
By means of its urine and excrement, copper becomes gold.
(48) The seeds of the Brahmavr̥kṣa, ground into powder and mixed with ghee, should be placed as before inside a grain-store and retrieved after one month. (49)
If one should always eat it, one pala at a time, for a year, one will become a conqueror of death;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall live for three days of Brahmā.

If one drinks [the substance] with equal parts [of other ingredients], fainting (mūrchā) will occur; one should sprinkle water on his face. Upon regaining consciousness, one should give him milk-rice; after a month, the man becomes a possessor of knowledge (jñānin).
In the second month he becomes equal to Śukra, and in the third he becomes like a diamond (vajra).
In the fourth month, one becomes capable of hearing from afar; in the fifth, one gains the power of flight through the sky.
In the sixth month, one becomes a creator oneself, possessing prowess equal to Śiva.
By practicing for a single year, one shall live until the end of the great kalpa.
One should cut down a very thick *brahmavṛkṣa* tree from its upper portion;
three cubits of it should be left protected at the bottom, and a hole should be made in its top.
This should be filled with ripe *dhātrī* fruits and then sealed shut with wood.
One should wrap the entire object with *kuśa* grass and then coat it with clay and cow dung; having wrapped it with a piece of cloth, one should then smear it again with clay and cow dung.
When it is dry, a "gaja-puta" (elephant-seal) firing should be applied, surrounded by wild blue lotuses (*araṇyakotpalas*).
Having extracted the fruits while they are still juicy and cool to the touch of one's own body,
one should place them in a vessel mixed with honey and clarified butter; staying within an underground chamber and subsisting on milk, one may eat those very fruits as desired and conquer old age.
Within two months, he will certainly see the earth as full of holes;
he shall live for as long as a day of Brahmā, casting off his skin like a serpent. (59) This is the ritual procedure for the white *pālāśa* tree.
The five parts of the white *pālāśa* tree ground into a powder with honey [is for] great strength;
[it is] indeed [to be taken] with *dhātrī* fruits.
One who has performed the cooking [of the elixir] perceives, after one month, holes in the earth and hidden treasures beneath it.
By constantly consuming a single *karṣa* [of this substance], death and old age are removed within a month. (60)
Within just one year, he becomes a perfected Siddha with the lifespan of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
One should always consume that seed one by one with goat’s ghee.
By rubbing the body with ashes for a month, one shall conquer death and old age.
The man shall live for as long as a day of Brahmā, and his body shall become divine.
Whatever other yogas exist in the red Brahmavṛkṣa, and whatever qualities it possesses, those very same shall belong to the practitioner in the white Pālāśa tree as well.
"Make [it] nectar, make [it] nectar; obeisance to Amṛtamālinī.
By means of this mantra, all yogas should be consumed after being consecrated seven times. This is the ritual manual for Muṇḍī.
Then, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight, or under the asterisms of Puṣya, Śravaṇa, or Revatī, having performed worship, one should extract the five parts of Muṇḍī.
That powder, dried in the shade, should be taken in a measure of one karṣa along with cow's milk.
By taking it for one year, one destroys old age and lives for three hundred years.
Through his urine and feces, copper attains the state of gold;
that powder, when licked with ghee, likewise produces wonderful strength.
Oṃ namo 'mṛtodbhavāya amṛtaṃ kuru kuru svāhā o hrāṃ saḥ. This is the mantra for consuming the medicinal herb; it is the ritual procedure for *devadālī*.
Then, one should powder the five parts of *devadālī* dried in the shade;
by licking a *karṣa* of this with honey and ghee, a man shall conquer death and old age within a year.
He shall live for a thousand kalpas and become equal to Rudra.
One karṣa of that powder should be drunk daily with auspicious water (śivāmbu).
Success arises as before within a year; there is no doubt about this.
That powder [is prepared] with equal parts of bākucī, vahni, sarpākṣī, and bhṛṅgarāja.
One should daily drink one *karṣa* of this powder with auspicious water (*śivāmbu*); after a year, it destroys death and old age, and one perceives the entire earth as having no hidden flaws.
A person should also daily drink [the powder] with the juices of *punarnavā* and *devadālī*.

One should drink one karṣa each of *devadālī* and *nirguṇḍī* with the water of Śiva; by doing so for one year, one destroys old age and may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Oṃ amṛtagaṇa rudragaṇāmbhaḥ svāhā.
And this is the mantra for seizing:
*namo bhagavate rudrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the mantra for binding the crest-lock (*śikhābandhana*) of the practitioner.
Oṃ cara ra ra ayaṃ bhakṣaṇamantraḥ śvetārkakalpaḥ. This is the mantra for consumption from the Śvetārka ritual manual.
During the Puṣya asterism, one should take the root of the white Arka plant and dry it in the shade;
then, one should drink a karṣa of its powder mixed with two palas of cow’s milk.
This destroys old age after six months, and one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
Take an equal amount of the juice of white *arka* leaves and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.

Having combined them, dry the mixture in the sun until it becomes a powder. Then cook this with four times as much milk over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a solid mass (*piṇḍatva*).
One karṣa of that should be licked with clarified butter; after a year, the result will be as previously described.
*Oṃ āṃ haṃ vāsaramāline svāhā*—this is the mantra for consumption.
Regarding the *hastikarṇa* preparation:
on the thirteenth lunar day of the moon, one should collect the leaf of the *hastikarṇa* tree;
having dried it in the shade, one should drink one *pala* of its powder with cow’s milk. (76)
By taking for only one year the five parts of *hastikarṇa* (elephant-ear), dried in the shade and powdered, a man destroys old age and may live for a *brahmadina*.
He should drink one *karṣa* daily with water for one month.
Then, it should be consumed sequentially with fermented gruel, buttermilk, curd, milk, clarified butter, and honey—one by one—for one month; this removes old age.
Possessing a body as firm as a diamond and great strength, one shall live for one and a half Brahma-days.
Oṃ, I take up the poison of pride within my sight, svāhā! This is the mantra for seizing the elephant-ear [herb].
Oṃ, make nectar, make nectar for those born from the Amṛtakuṭī, svāhā!
With this, one should perform worship:
*Oṃ amṛtodbhavāya amṛtaṃ kuru kuru nityaṃ namo namaḥ*. This is the mantra for consumption.
One *karṣa* [of the following]:
*kha*. [The ritual procedure] for those born from the womb of nectar (*amṛtakukṣijātānām*), *kha*.
[is] the ritual manual for *rudantī* (*rudantīkalpaḥ*).

then add half as much *muśalī* powder, half as much *muśalī* again [in total], and one-third as much of the three fruits (*phalatraya*). [These should be processed] with oil extracted from the roots of *katakā* using a *pātālayantra* apparatus.

One should perform an increase starting from one *karṣa* up to the end of a *pala*; by increasing in this manner for a year, one destroys old age, and one's lifespan shall become equal to a day of Brahmā.
Indeed, this is known as Siddhayoga, which makes the bodies of men like adamant.
The ritual for *nirguṇḍī*:
on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, one should collect the bark from the root of *nirguṇḍī* in the morning;
having dried it in the shade and then powdered it, one should always drink one *karṣa* of it.
By using one *pala* of goat urine for six months, one becomes immortal.
By practicing this for just one year, a man becomes equal to Śiva.
That powder, stirred with milk, honey, and clarified butter, should be kept in a smooth vessel.

That powder—consisting of triphalā, muṇḍī, bhṛṅgī, nimba, guḍūcī, and vacā—in equal parts, one pala of this powder should be licked with honey and ghee. Within a year, it destroys death and old age; one shall live for three days of Brahmā.

One should cook the juice extracted from *nirguṇḍī* leaves in a vessel over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of jaggery; when drunk, it induces vomiting and purgation, and worms emerge from one's mouth, nose, eyes, and ears. (90)
One shall destroy diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) within seven days;
after three months, it destroys old age, and one shall live for three hundred years.
*Oṃ namo māya gaṇapataye bhūpataye kuberāya svāhā*—this is the mantra for consumption.
Five parts of *bhallātaka*, *abhayā*, *vīrā*, the fruit of *kākatuṇḍī*, and *vacā* constitute several formulations for elixirs (*rasāyana*) that extend life by five years.
Lāṅgalī, nimba leaves, and sahadevī— taking equal parts of these,
one should carefully extract the oil using the pātālayantra.
One should drink half a pala of that oil combined with the root of nīlikā.
It destroys premature graying from the very beginning; it constitutes a day of Brahmā for one’s lifespan.
If half a niṣka of oil is applied as nasal drops (nasya), the same result as mentioned before shall be obtained.
One prastha of black cumin seeds and an equal amount of liquid extracted from *bhṛṅgarāja* [should be used].

One should take half a *prastha* each of yaṣṭī and blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and one-quarter *prastha* of oil from sesame; one should cook all these together in one vessel. When only the oil remains, it should be taken and used as a nasal medication (*nasya*). || 95-96 ||

One should administer nasal drops (*nasya*) with *aṅkolla* oil, which removes death and old age; by using half a *niṣka* or one *niṣka* [of this oil], one shall live for three hundred years. Having ground the fruit of *kākamācī*, one should drink one *karṣa* with water.
Within a year, it destroys gray hair; such a lifespan would be a day for Brahmā. 98.
Equal parts of *guḍūcī*, *muśalī*, *muṇḍī*, *nirguṇḍī*, *śatāvarī*, and *vijayā* should be powdered and combined with sugar, honey, and clarified butter. 99.
One should eat two karṣas daily; after one year, one will conquer graying hair.
As stated by Gorakṣanātha, one shall live for three Brahma-days. (100) This is the ritual procedure for *śunaka-śālmalikā*.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having encircled a *śunaka-śālmali* tree with black threads at night while reciting the Aghora mantra, and having offered a black goat as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*),
one should mutter the Aghora mantra there until eight thousand repetitions are completed.
One should take the root bark of that [plant], dry it in the shade, and reduce it to powder.

a man shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live for the length of a Brahma-day.

he shall live until the end of the kalpa, possessing the speed of the wind and great strength.

The fruits of *kākatuṇḍī*, the root of *brahmī* and *aśvagandhā*,
the leaves of blue *koraṇṭaka*, and *triphalā*— taking these in equal parts,
one should prepare a powder and saturate it with the juices of *kanyā* for seven days.
One should dry it in the shade and prepare it mixed with sugar, honey, and ghee;
by eating two karṣas daily for the duration of a year, one conquers old age.
Possessing a great body and great strength, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.

Oṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ saḥ saḥ saḥ, O immortal one, O showerer of nectar, O reviver by nectar, O bestower of all desires, the Blessed Lord Somarāja commands: svāhā! This is the mantra for consumption. The formulation of Triphalā and others consists of triphalā, bākucī seeds, pippalī, and aśvagandhā.
Having made everything equal, one should lick a *pala* of the powder with honey and ghee;
after a year, it destroys death and old age, and one shall live for three days of Brahmā.
One should consume it while reciting this mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ saḥ svāhā*.
Regarding the mercury formulations in the medicinal herb compendia:
one should consume a single *guñjā* of processed mercury combined with its counteragent; the result shall be a hundredfold.
By the power of the lord of mercury (rasendra), one shall quickly attain success.
Regarding the mantra-yoga in the alchemical preparations (rasāyana-kalpa):
the practitioner of mantras, wearing the bone-seal (asthi-mudrā), [should recite] one hundred thousand [times] at the cremation ground.
By reciting it, one destroys great fear; it bestows accomplishment and is an elixir.
Merely by consuming it, one may live as long as the moon and stars;
invincible to gods and demons, one may even shake the mountains. (113–114)
Oṃ hrīṃ Mahābhayeru! Regarding the procedure for the administration of the elixir (*rasāyana*):
on an auspicious day such as the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun, or other primary auspicious days, [one should perform it] according to the ritual procedures for mantra and worship.

For the sake of accomplishment, one who observes celibacy should consume for success the fruit, leaf, flower, root, petal, juice, or even the entire body of divine medicinal herbs—all of which must be fresh;
milk-rice or water-rice is the beneficial diet, and all other food should be avoided. 115.
Thus ends the fourth instruction, titled "Various Rasāyanas," in the section on Rasāyana from the *Śrīrasaratnākara* composed by the Siddha Śrī Nityanātha, son of Śrī Pārvatī.
Now begins the fifth instruction:
"Udvartana (massage/scrub) is supreme for removing gray hair in men."

I shall describe, through many methods, this well-proven [practice] seen by the path of direct experience— [a practice] that brings beauty, produces happiness, is a delight to the eyes, is suitable for the elderly, and is easily accomplished. 1.
For the purpose of destroying wrinkles and graying hair, there is an ointment made of mercury and other ingredients.
One should grind equal parts of mercury and sulfur with breast milk, along with *viṣṇukrāntā*, *meghanādā*, *sarpākṣī*, and *munimuṇḍikā*. (2)
One should grind these with their juices in a mortar for a day, then extract them; one should add barley powder and sesame seeds, each equal in measure to the juice,
mix everything together with ghee and honey, and preserve it.
By this, anointment properly destroys wrinkles and gray hair.
After one year, one will possess a divine body and live for a thousand years.
This is the anointment with the root of Vajrakāpālinī and other ingredients for the purpose of destroying wrinkles and gray hair.
Equal parts of the root of Vajrakāpālinī and mercury should be ground together with the water of Śivā for three days; from this ointment, as before, comes the result:
the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair through the application of the Utpalādi ointment.
Take blue lotuses with their roots and mercury in equal parts;
grind them together for seven days in a mortar using one's own *aśivā* water (urine), which is a supreme strengthener of the body.
One should rub the body with that very [substance], and the result arises as before.
For the purpose of destroying wrinkles and graying hair, there is an ointment of mercury and other ingredients; one part of mercury should be mixed with an equal amount of the root of *brahmadaṇḍī*.
Having cast [the ingredients] together, one should grind them for seven days with one's own urine.
By means of this, one should rub the body; the fruit previously described arises.
This is the sulphur formulation for the purpose of destroying wrinkles and graying hair.
Sulfur should be infused with mustard oil for a period of days under the heat of the sun.
One should always consume half a *pala* of that; it makes the bodies of men divine.
After one year, the body becomes like gold and free from wrinkles.

For the purpose of rejuvenation, one who daily licks a karṣa of kuṣṭha powder mixed with honey and ghee will, after a year, possess a divine body with a fragrance like that of the śatapuṣpa flower. 11.
For the purpose of destroying grey hair, there is this formulation of magnetite and other substances:
one should prepare an equal quantity of all these—powdered magnetite combined with oil, honey, and clarified butter, along with the fruit of *kākatuṇḍī*. (12)
Having sealed it in a vessel, one should leave it for a month in a heap of grain and then remove it;
with this one should smear the head and indeed administer it as a nasal drop (nasya).
Within three days, the hair becomes like a bee [in color], and this lasts for half a year.
For the purpose of destroying grey hair, there is this formulation of lead and other substances:
one pala of powdered lead (nāga), two palas of powdered conch shell, and one niṣka of powdered harītakī (pathyā);
all of this should be ground together for a period of one day.
Having first bathed with care, one should apply [the substance] mixed with sour curds to the head;
one should massage it for half a ghaṭikā, wrap the head with castor leaves, and after binding it with a cloth, perform the morning ablution.
Having thus diligently performed this for three days, one should dye the hair;
for the purpose of hair-dyeing, there is this formulation of nīlikā and other ingredients:
the five components consisting of nīlikā, bhṛṅga, triphalā, and iron powder. (17)
Having prepared equal amounts of all [the ingredients], one should grind them finely with urine and *iḍā* for half a day; with that paste, the hair-dyeing is performed as previously described.
This is the formulation of *guñjā* and other substances for the purpose of hair-dyeing.
The seeds of *guñjā*, excluding the husk, along with *kuṣṭha*, *elā*, and *devadāru*—
these should be powdered in equal parts and soaked for one day in the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
Then, all of this should be cooked over a gentle fire in four times the amount of oil.
By that massage, the hair becomes colored like a bumblebee.
For the purpose of coloring the hair, there is a formulation involving elephant tusks and other ingredients: burnt elephant tusk should be mixed with an equal amount of *rasāñjana*.
Having ground that with goat’s milk, application as an ointment results in the dyeing of the hair.
Regarding the formulation of triphalā and other ingredients for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
triphalā, iron powder, black earth, and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should confine the juice of sugarcane stalks in a vessel for one month;
by applying that as a paste, one may dye the hair for up to five months.
This is a formulation using iron dross and other substances for the purpose of hair-dyeing.
Having ground iron rust, *japā* flowers, and *dhātrī* fruit in equal parts,
hair that is anointed with this for three days will become like a bumblebee.
One *prastha* of *bhṛṅgarāja* juice and oil produced from black sesame seeds—
One should grind all these together with an equal amount of *nīlikā* juice for one watch (three hours); applying that as a paste for three days will result in the coloring of the hair.
[25] This is the formulation of vermilion and other substances for the purpose of coloring the hair.

Equal parts of vermilion powder and soap, these two ground together with water and applied as a paste, instantly dyes the hair black. The following is a formulation for dyeing the hair using *śatapuṣpā* and other ingredients.
One should grind together śatapuṣpā, kākamācī, black sesame seeds, and gorocana for one day in an iron vessel with the water of a *śiva* (auspicious) plant.
One should apply that paste for three days, and it will result in the coloring of the hair.
The formulation of powders and other substances for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
powder of *sarjī*, *yavakṣāra*, and *siddhārtha* mixed with *kāñjika* and rubbed with the juices of *nāgapuṣpa*; from the application of that, dyeing occurs.
The preparation for dyeing the hair with indigo and other substances:
having ground together equal parts of indigo leaves, green vitriol (kāsīsa), the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
curd, and iron powder, that paste is for the dyeing of the hair.
The formulation of powders and other substances for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
powder, vermilion, charcoal, combined with the bulb of the plantain (kadalī),
should be rubbed in an iron vessel with an iron pestle using the juices of citron fruits.
Then, after a single day, it should be applied as a paste; this will be a hair-dye.
Regarding the preparation of *kuraṇṭaka* leaves and other ingredients for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
one should grind the leaves of the *kuraṇṭaka* with *nāgamuṣṭī*.
One should apply this ointment for three days, and the blackening of the hair occurs.
Regarding the formulation of mango-stone and other ingredients for the purpose of blackening the hair:
mango-stone, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *bhṛṅgī*, *priyaṅgu*, and citron.

Take equal parts of indigo, lotus stalks, snake, and powdered iron; having prepared this paste, one should saturate a vessel made of kāntaloha with nimba oil for exactly one month. Then, by applying a coating of it, a dyeing effect is produced.
A formulation of *kākamācī* and other ingredients for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
equal parts of *kākamācī* seeds and black sesame seeds; one should extract their oil using a press, and that oil used as an errhine (*nasya*) dyes the hair. (35)
Cow's ghee, the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *mayūraśikhā* should be cooked over a gentle fire; this oil for the eyes serves as a nasal drop (*nasya*) that dyes the hair black. (36)

For the purpose of dyeing the hair, one should administer as a nasal drop (nasya) one karṣa of the juice of the hibiscus flower mixed with honey; this will dye the hair within seven days. This is the procedure for all nasal applications. || 37 ||

For the purpose of dyeing the hair, one should grind equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and iron powder with water; this should then be mixed with an equal amount of oil and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*. (38)
One should cook it until only the oil remains, then seal it in a greased vessel; having buried it underground for one month, one should smear the head with that [preparation].
Then, having wrapped it with the leaves of *kāravallī*, one should bind it with a cloth.
One should eat milk in a windless place and wash [the head] with water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
This application should be performed daily for seven days;
it is known as "staining the skull" and lasts for a lifetime, without a doubt.
Regarding the formulation of *kākatuṇḍī* and other substances for the purpose of dyeing the hair:
the seeds of *kākatuṇḍī* combined with the seeds of *siryālī*, this powder should be infused for four days with the juices of *niguṇḍī*. (42)
Then, having extracted oil from *japā* flowers using a subterranean apparatus (*pātālayantra*), the hair becomes dyed by an application of that oil.
One should wrap it with castor leaves and remain in a windless place while consuming a diet of milk.
If one performs a bath with *kāñjika* daily for seven days,
there is no doubt that for as long as one lives, the hair will be free of grayness.
For the purpose of dyeing the hair, there is this formulation using *bhṛṅgarāja* and other ingredients.
Having ground equal parts of *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kācamācī*, and *jalamaṇḍavī* into a paste and formed them into cakes (*apūpikā*), one should cook them in oil; once cooked,
one should grind them again with oils, and this ointment will be for the coloring of the hair.
By following the sequence as before, that result will be achieved within seven days.
For the purpose of dyeing the hair, there is a formulation of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and other ingredients:
at night, the three fruits should be smeared onto a vessel made of magnetite (*ayaskānta*). (47)

One should apply a paste of black cumin seeds together with the juice of *mṛṅgarāja* to the hair in the morning; by doing this for three weeks, the same result as before is produced. (48) This is the application of black cumin for the purpose of dyeing the hair.
One should place black cumin in a buffalo horn and seal it;
having buried it in the mud at the front of one's house, one should extract it after six months.
That [substance] quickly becomes black; one *karṣa* of it should be applied to the head.
One should wrap it according to the previous method; it will become a coloring for the skull, resembling bumblebee collyrium for as long as one lives—of this there is no doubt.
[The seed-syllable] is equal. kha.
A water-based cosmetic preparation; a cake made with *sarpākṣī*;
a formulation of indigo and other substances for the purpose of dyeing the hair.
Indigo leaf, bhṛṅgarāja, the three myrobalans (triphalā),
black iron, the seeds of madana, the flower of koraṇṭaka, the bark of arjuna, powder, and the mud from the roots of the lotus. || 51-52 ||

One should cast everything equally into an iron vessel and seal it; after one fortnight, one should take the paste out from the vessel and bury it in the ground. To the paste, four times as much oil should be added, and to the oil, four times as much liquid.
One should add the [decoction] of *bhṛṅga* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and cook it until only the oil remains.
To test it, one should drop a crane feather; when it turns black, the preparation is perfected and should be poured into an iron vessel.
One should apply it to that [hair] for one month; thereafter, one should smear the hair.
For six months they remain, resembling a swarm of bees.
This is a preparation of lead and other substances for the purpose of dyeing the hair.
Using sturdy sticks made from the wood of the vāsā, palāśa, ciñcā, or aśvattha trees,
one should stir the mercury contained in the vessel until it becomes thickened (mūrcchita).
Then, taking one pala of that [mercury] and two palas of iron powder—
Three palas of powdered triphalā and one pala of dried powder from the fruit-skin of pomegranate—
having cooked all these together with an equal amount of kāñjika in a vessel until slightly thickened, one should pour it into an iron container.
Having added the juice extracted from *bhṛṅgarāja* and *kuraṇṭaka*, one should expose it to the sun for twenty-one days with diligence, adding the juice again and again.
Then, one should preserve it; by applying it as an ointment, there shall be the coloring of the hair.

Whether the ointments mentioned or those not mentioned have been applied, one should wrap the head with castor leaves; bathing at night and [avoiding it] during the day— this method is praised as a formulation for whitening the hair.
One should soak *abhayā* fruits in *vajrīkṣīra* for seven days;
by applying an ointment of oil mixed with their powder, the hair indeed becomes white, and all the body hairs become the color of a conch shell. (62)
One should soak white sesame seeds with vajra-milk for seven days. Having extracted the oil from them, by anointing [the teeth] with it, they indeed become white.
Likewise, the powder of gaurī-āmalaka should be processed seven times with vajra-milk.
By applying that ointment, the hair becomes white;
one should apply vermilion and white crystal together with water as a paste. By that application, the hairs indeed become very white.
One should macerate one month’s worth of Māgadhī powder with the milk of a Vajrī cow.
This is the supreme method for whitening the semen of men, horses, elephants, and stallions.
[One should also use] Indragopa, Tailinī, Tālaka, and the two types of Rajanī.
One should powder equal parts of realgar and soak it for three days with the milk of the *snuk* plant,
and for three days in the hot sun with the milky sap of the *arka* plant.
Then, one should soak it for seven days in the juices of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd.
Then, having placed [the hair] inside a pumpkin, one should extract it after a month.
One should smear all the body hairs and the head hair with oil for three days and wrap them with *arka* leaves; they will then become white in color.
When bathing has been performed and the hair is dry, and after an ointment has been applied at night, one should wrap [the head] with the aforementioned petals;
then, in the morning, one should bathe with curd and sesame seeds. In this same manner, the application of the ointment should be continued for three days.

Thus ends the fifth instruction, titled "The Chapter on Body Rubs and Hair Dyeing," in the section on elixirs (*rasāyana*) within the *Rasaratnākara* composed by the Siddha Śrī Nityanātha, son of Pārvatī.
Now begins the sixth instruction:
For those who possess women skilled in dalliance, attached to passion,
bold, devoted to desire, with eyes like deer and faces like the orb of the moon;
For them, I shall describe the abundant increase of virility that bestows the pleasure of passion; even a hundred intoxicated, perfected, and steadfast ones are satisfied by such [a preparation].
This is the aphrodisiac *makaradhvajarasa*.
The ashes of vajra, gold, copper, mercury, mica, and iron, each progressively more potent than the last, when combined with water,
satisfy even a hundred such women in that accomplishment.
All [the ingredients] should be ground with the juices of *kanyā* and the juices of *śālmali* for three days.
Having sealed that [mixture] inside a glass vessel, one should cook it in sand for three days.
Then, that paste [should be processed] with decoctions of *muśalī* combined with the milks of *vajra* and *arka*.
One should rub it in a mortar for one day, seal it, and then roast it in a *bhūdhara* furnace.

After removing it after one watch (*yāma*), one should powder it and mix it with equal parts of sugar, black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), and the three aromatics (*trijātaka*). Then, one should always consume one *māṣa* of this mixture.
One should administer half a *pala* of a powder made from equal parts of *māgadhī*, *muśalī*, *yaṣṭī*, and the seeds of *vānarī*, mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and cow’s milk; by doing so,
one does not lose one's vigor even while sporting with a thousand women.
By its regular use, one shall possess a firm body; this mercury is the "Makaradhvaja" (the Fish-bannered God).
This "Manodaya" elixir is an aphrodisiac:
pure mercury and an equal amount of sulfur [are mixed] with the juice of red lotus petals.
One should grind the *yāma* [of mercury] again and add an equal amount of sulfur (*gandha*) to it.

Having ground it for one day with the previous liquids, one should again add half as much sulfur as the mercury and grind it for another day; then, one should seal it inside a glass flask (*kācakūpī*).
Having cooked it for one day in a sand-bath (vālukāyantra) and removed it, one should grind it into a powder;
then one should saturate it with the decoction of Bhūkūṣmāṇḍī for seven days.
Dried in the shade, one should always consume one niṣka of this, equal in weight to white sugar.
One should always drink at night an equal measure of hemp root with its seeds, musalī, and sugar— half a pala each— in cow's milk; this elixir,
called Madanodaya, increases virility infinitely.
The aphrodisiac *Madaneśvararasa* is prepared by grinding purified mercury with an equal amount of sulfur using the juices of *badarī*, *citraka*,
and *aṅkolla* in a heated mortar for three days.
One should place [the mercury] upon a ball of freshly slaughtered goat meat and sew it up; then,
one should slowly cook that ball in an iron vessel with sesame oil until the meat turns red, at which point one should extract the mercury.
This essence, Madaneśvara, should be processed with decoctions of *muśalī* for three days and then combined with sugar;
one should consume one *niṣka* of it daily for two days.

One should drink one *pala* of powdered *vidārīkanda* with milk and clarified butter. This elixir known as *kāmakalā*, which acts as an aphrodisiac (*vājīkara*), enables one to constantly enjoy a hundred women; by abandoning it, however, one falls into blindness.
One should grind equal parts of "dead" mercury (mṛtābhra), mercury (pārada), and gold for three days with decoctions of muśalī and triphalā,
as well as with the infusions of vājigandhā and the juices extracted from the roots of kadalī. Then, having enclosed that mass in a sealed vessel, one should subject it to puṭapāka.
Having extracted it for just one day in *bhūdhara* [mud], one should then grind it;
having likewise sealed it with the aforementioned fluxes for one day, one should cook it in a crucible (*puṭa*).
It should be ground again and cooked again; in this manner, one should cook it through eight *puṭas*.

One should eat two niṣkas daily of the resin produced from the *śālmalī* tree mixed with sugar; this will cause one to attract hundreds of women. Afterwards, one should drink half a *pala* of *markaṭī* seeds with cow’s milk.
One should perform a full-body massage with *śālmalī* juice mixed with barley;
this elixir known as *Kāmakalā* bestows great virility upon men. It is an aphrodisiac, the *Kāmadeva-rasa*.
Three parts of dead mercury and one part of dead gold should be rubbed for a day with the juices of the *kadalī* root and the juices of *śālmalī*,
and for another day with cow’s milk; then it should be cooked for a single moment in clarified butter.
Into the middle of that, having added sugar, grapes, āmalakī, plantain fruit,
honey, cow’s milk, musalī, black gram, and the seeds of kokilākṣa—
each four times the quantity of the mercury— one should grind it with the juices of śālmalī.
All of that, for a single day, becomes the essence of Kāmadeva; one should always consume a quantity of exactly one niṣka, and afterwards drink cow’s milk.
By this, one's phallus shall become firm during sexual union, and one shall cause the assembly of women to melt with passion.

One should rub the mercury (sūtaka) with the menstrual blood of women at the onset of their menses for a day; this is an aphrodisiac (vājīkara) elixir that increases the passion for pleasure. One should likewise grind dead copper, silver, and sulfur in equal parts for a day.
Having consumed a niṣka of sugar mixed with honey and clarified butter, one should drink milk.
This is known as *ratikāmarasa*, which is beneficial for those who desire pleasure and for lovers.
[One should also take] the root of *vānarī*, wheat, and the seeds of *kokilākṣa*.
One should cook all these ingredients—māṣa beans stirred with sugarcane juice and ghee—and from that, one should prepare *vaṭaka* balls; one should eat two of them daily.
This proven preparation, when used as a post-digestive drink (*anupāna*), will delight a hundred women through its consumption.

Take purified mercury equal in quantity to sulphur and grind them for three days with the juices of white water-lilies (kahlāra); having sealed the mixture in a crucible, it should be cooked in a *vālukāyantra* until it reaches the state of *yāma*. This is the intoxicant-boosting *madavardhana-rasa*, which acts as an aphrodisiac (*vājīkara*).

It should be infused for one day with the juices of red agastya and combined with sugar; one should always consume a quantity of one niṣka. This elixir increases virility. [One may also take] the testicles of a goat cooked in milk and combined with sesame and sugar.
One may eat it as desired and enjoy a hundred passionate women;
this is the *anaṅgasundarī* pill, which acts as an aphrodisiac.
Two *pala*s each of pure mercury and auspicious sulfur [are required]. (33)
One *karṣa* of killed gold, one *pala* of killed copper,
and four *niṣkas* of silver ash— having ground all these together with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for a day,
one should seal it and cook it in a *bhūdhara* [digester] for a day; then one should extract it.
Having ground these with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should eat a pill the size of a jujube fruit;
it is known as Anaṅgasundarī and enables one to enjoy a hundred women.
Furthermore, the powder of the root of the śālmalī tree, combined with honey and sugar [is effective].
One should consume one *pala* [of this] and afterwards drink milk with sugar;
this is the aphrodisiac *Kāmanāyaka-rasa*.
Pure mercury should be rubbed with juices derived from *śālmali* for one fortnight. (37)
One should rub pure fragrance with those liquids separately for three weeks;
then, having combined these two in equal parts, one should rub them again with ghee for four *yāmas*.
One should bind that mass in a cloth and cook it with ghee for two *yāmas*.
Then, one should grind it with the juices of the Śālmalī tree for three days.

One should place it inside a glass vessel (kāca-kūpī) within a sand-bath apparatus (vālukā-yantra) and cook it; one should pour the juice of the Śālmalī into the interior of the vessel for the duration of those days.
Having extracted it while still moist and mixed with an equal amount of sugar, one should always consume a quantity of one *niṣka*; this elixir is the leader of all desires.
Following this, one should drink one *pala* of *muśalī* with milk and sugar.
It can agitate a thousand amorous women within the blink of an eye.
This aphrodisiac, the essence of the full moon,
consists of three parts of purified mercury and one part of copper powder.
Having made a paste, one should then enclose it within the interior of a plantain bulb;
smeared with clay and dried, one should cook it for one day over a fire of cow-dung.
In this manner, one should cook it for seven days, placing it in each successive bulb for one day at a time.
Having extracted it, one should bind it in a firm cloth of four layers and cook it while immersed in the blood of a goat smeared with the flesh of a small snail;
this should be done for three days in a *dolāyantra*, adding blood again and again.

One should cook it for three days in a dolāyantra (suspended-pot apparatus) using the juices or decoctions of guḍūcī, gajapippalī, kadalī, kokilākṣaka, gokṣurī, vānarī root, and jātī root. || 46-47 ||
Then, one should cook it likewise for a day in milk mixed with sugar;
having removed it, it should be rubbed with a decoction of *muśalī* for four watches (yāmas). This elixir, named Pūrṇendu, should be consumed along with meat and sugar.

Gokṣura, the seeds of vānarī, guḍūcī, gajapippalī, the seeds of kokilākṣa, the marrow from cotton seeds, śatāvarī, and the entire fruit of the plantain tree— all these should be taken in equal parts. || 49-50 ||

One should take one *pala* of equal parts of all [the ingredients] mixed with white [sugar] and stirred with honey; this should be licked, and thereafter cow's milk should be drunk as a post-digestive drink (*anupāna*).
Thus, one enjoys the company of a thousand passionate women like the god of love himself. || 51 ||
The aphrodisiac Madanakāma-rasa consists of lotus seeds, kaseru, the bulb, the stalk, and the pericarp;
as well as musalī, bhṛṅgarāja, grapes, and the ripe fruit of śleṣmātaka. || 52 ||
Vijayā, markaṭī, māṣas, śaṇa seeds, and indeed sesame;
suśītalā, kokilākṣa seeds, bhūkūṣmāṇḍī, and śatāvarī.
Śṛṅgāṭa, cirbhiṭa, the seeds of phaṇī, and aśvagandhikā—having powdered all of these together in equal parts, one should take a separate quarter-portion [of each];
then, one should mix in purified mercury (sūta) amounting to one-eighth of that quarter-portion. || 54–55 ||
One should add camphor equal to one-eighth part of the mercury;
each of the four spices (cāturjātaka) should be double the amount of the camphor.
White sugar equal to the mercury should be added, and the mixture should be rubbed with the juice of plantain leaves for one day.
One should cook that pill in a *ḍāmara* apparatus with fire increased in stages.

At the end of the day, when it has become firm at the top, it should be taken; having been firmly rubbed with the juice of plantain and mixed with an equal amount of sugar, one should always consume a single *māṣa*.

In the vicinity is the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the god Puruṣeśvara.
Two trees, the Guñjā and the Riṣṭhaka, stand there; by eating their leaves, one becomes immortal at that very moment.
Likewise, there is the Hastiśilā stone there; one should dig to the south of it.
Then one should see [a stone] the size of a cubit, shaped like a rose-apple fruit (jambūphala).
That stone is described there as being perceivable by touch with effort;
it is renowned by the name Hastiśiras, and that very thing is the Hastiśilā.
One yojana to the south of that place stands the famous Chāyāchatra, which is a form of Śiva as proclaimed by Śiva;
that sacred field is one hundred cubits in measure and perfectly circular.
Whoever goes there, he is not seen by anyone below.
Having gone to the Arjuna tree,
the perfected one (siddha) becomes equal to Rudra and sports throughout the three worlds.
Alternatively, one may accomplish the eight well-known Siddhis from afar.
Mercury, gold, and mica should be ground together, each succeeding ingredient being double the quantity of the preceding;
then, one should carefully encase that globule with the three metals in their proper order.
Having tied that cloth with another cloth, one should bind it firmly to the tip of a bamboo pole;
having consecrated it with the Kālī-mantra, one should place it under a parasol in the shade. In a single moment, that tip of the bamboo becomes a pill.
The practitioner should hold in his mouth that which bestows the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
Likewise, having bound realgar and mica within a bamboo tube, he should insert it; whoever has his eyes anointed with these two beholds the treasure buried in the earth.
Having bound the sword with a bamboo cane and consecrated it with the previously mentioned mantra, one should hold that sword in the hand; one will then become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Having bound *gorocanā* in a cloth, one should place it there within the bamboo cane.
With that very [substance], one should make a tilaka; having seen it, one deludes the world.
Having cast *srotoñjana* and collyrium into that same [substance] as before, he whose eyes are anointed with it cannot be seen even by the gods.
Having cast the sandals by that yoga, he should wear them on his feet;
then, wherever he desires, he shall go there at that very moment.
Likewise, having cast a red cloth there and wrapped himself in it, the practitioner—
It becomes invisible when [the cloth] is properly applied, but it is seen once the cloth is removed.

Having prepared a ball of mercury mixed with mica and gold, one should place it at the tip of a bamboo stalk while reciting the mantra; that will then become a "touch-mercury" (sparśavedhī). || 54–55 ||
At the western gate of Śrīśaila is the deity named Brahmeśvareśvara;
they say that his liṅga is called Sparśa, and Durgā is likewise present right there.
As for the ninth flight of steps leading down to the river, it is situated in such a manner.
One should behold the one of mung-bean color standing at the gate of the God.
To the southwest of Brahmeśvara is situated a grove of tamarind trees;
in that grove stands a pool, and there resides Caṇḍikā.
Standing on one leg beneath a *ciñcā* tree, one should pluck a leaf from the tree, tie it in a cloth, and cast it into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); there, one should perform the ritual bath.
At the conclusion of the bath, a small bundle (*poṭalī*) should be taken; all those [beings] become fish.
One should cook those [roots] with their wood; one should discard the neck, the tail, and the head.
Having dedicated one portion to the deity, the second shall belong to the guest;
the practitioner, having eaten the third, becomes faint for a moment.
At that very moment, one becomes perfected; one sees the earth as having gaps, attains freedom from old age and death, and cannot be harmed even by the gods.
To the north of Alampura, there is a village called Bhīmapāduka.
One should dig the earth for a distance of one cubit beside that village;
there, stones curved like serpents will be found to the touch.
This deity is renowned as Yogeśvarī, who resides in Alampura.
In front of the Goddess, there is a beautiful cave; one should bury the earth in its center.
Stones resembling frogs should be taken along with cat excrement.
Having mixed these together, one should cast them into tin; that tin will attain the state of silver.
The wise man should eat those stones together with honey and clarified butter.
At the northern gate of Śrīśaila, there is a deity named Maheśa; a *bhramarāmra* tree stands there, and its ripe fruits indeed [should be consumed].
One should burst them open; then bees, together with their lives, emerge.
Having recognized this sign, one should abandon those bees.
One should ripen the fruits in milk and drink milk as much as desired.
By that, a slight fainting may occur; thereafter, upon regaining consciousness, one should drink again.
One should practice in this manner for three weeks, and the person shall possess a vajra-body, freed from wrinkles and grey hair, and live as long as the moon and stars.
A man shall become a knower of all speech and possess the speed of the wind;
by that very single mango fruit from which the bees have been removed, he can certainly cause a thousand sprouts of the *vaṅga* tree to wither away.
By casting [it], one attains longevity; this is the truth spoken by the Lord.
Having perforated that fruit and then extracted the bee from it, one should take one karṣa of pure mercury and an equal amount of black mica.
Having cast [the powder] into that [liquid], one should cover the mouth and smear it with clay and cow dung.
Once dried in the shade, one should cook it for a watch (three hours) with decoctions derived from mangoes.
When it has cooled naturally, the pill situated within the fruit should be extracted.
When placed in the mouth, it grants the power of flight; when exceedingly potent, it bestows invisibility.
When processed in a decoction, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati and may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
One should pierce silver, copper, or lead with a ten-millionth part [of the essence].
One should place black soot and pure mercury into that fruit as before;
likewise, one should coat it with clay and cow dung and roast it in a forest lotus-leaf crucible (puṭapāka).
When it has cooled naturally, its juice should be taken along with honey and ghee.
By always consuming a single *guñjā* seed for one month, a man becomes a child;
such a hero lives for the duration of a day of Brahmā, endowed with the strength of nine elephants,
renowned throughout the world, and worthy of worship with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacārakaiḥ*).
By means of the mantra *oṃ huṃ phaṭ*, which is free from conceptual construction, the practitioners,
having gazed toward the western direction and into the intermediate space, shall at that very moment behold divine celestial chariots; thus, a great conviction arises.
Then, in the western direction, the wise one should go and cross a river;
there a cave is seen, and he should enter it facing west.
He should travel alone and free from conceptual thought for three yojanas.
A plantain grove extending five yojanas is seen;
in its center is a very vast lake filled with water,
and in the middle of that is a throne resembling pure crystal.
Upon seeing him, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff and recite the mantra:
*Oṃ hrīṃ vidyāvāgīśvarādhipataye hrīṃ oṃ svāhā*.
Having performed the ritual bath with diligence, one should subsequently recite it one hundred thousand times.
Having eaten as much as desired of bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth,
one then beholds the Supreme Lord upon the throne, resembling pure crystal, with four arms and three eyes. || 84-85 ||
By means of hymns, mantras, and prostrations, bowing down again and again, he indeed grants the practitioner whatever boon is desired; of this there is no doubt.
There are one hundred shrines there, as well as one hundred and nine wells.
There are that many fire-altars made of wood, as well as gardens called Nandana groves;
likewise, nine hundred step-wells exist in the plantain forest.
There are as many doorways as there are holes, and likewise as many wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas).
Right there, a yakṣiṇī named Maukalī stands manifest; she says: "Give me food, if you desire what you wish for."
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should say to her: "I shall give [it to you]";
the wise man should cause milk-rice or fruit-food to be offered before her.
She says: "This is my son; hold him to your breast for a moment."

When you do not release [the breath] upon the ground, then I shall grant you the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi); of this there is no doubt. Alternatively, if it is released at the end of the meal, I perform the withdrawal; therefore, protect it with great effort. 91–92.
In this manner, the heroic practitioner should act so that he may attain accomplishment;
he should go toward the northern direction for half a *yojana* to that lake.
There lies the divine forest named Nandana, filled with flowers.
By the mere scent of these flowers, hunger and thirst do not exist.
Alternatively, one should eat one fruit from it as is appropriate;
by the mere act of eating that, a person becomes possessed of a vajra-body.
One should go a quarter-yojana toward the southern part of the lake;
there, the Nandana grove filled with pomegranates is seen. A perfected one (siddha) who eats its fruit shall live for a thousand yugas.
One should go half a krośa toward the eastern part of that lake.
There lies the dark Nandana forest, filled with dhātrī fruits;
by eating those fruits, one shall live for three hundred kalpas.
One should go one yojana to the western part of that lake;
there, the Nandana grove is seen, filled with bilva fruits.
A hero who eats those fruits shall live as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars endure.
In that delightful Nandana grove, there shall be a linga of blue color.
One should enter through the northern gate; there, a serpent of great strength is seen—fierce, with seven hoods, and extremely terrifying.
One should perform obeisance to him, utter "hruṃ hruṃ," and extract [the mantra];
by pronouncing the syllable "huṃ," he then speaks these words: "I grant you invisibility. (102)
Go to the western gate; there is a divine maiden there. O great hero, the practitioner should go there while reciting the mantra.
Being pleased, she will give him a necklace, but she does not grant entrance.
One should wear that necklace around one's neck; one will then become Vāgīśvara himself.
Then, one should go to the southern gate, where there is a terrifying figure with disheveled hair, crooked eyes, a mace in hand, and clad in the directions as his garment.
Upon seeing the blue-colored Kṣetrapāla, one should recite the mantra:
*ha hā he he haṃ hruṃ phaṭ huṃ svāhā*.
By the recitation of this mantra, Kṣetrapāla becomes propitiated.
It bestows the siddhi of the Khecarī, but never entry.
Then, in the eastern quarter, the gate is seen there; the practitioner should worship Gaṇeśvara and enter from there.
A divine bow and a beautiful linga are seen there;
one should worship Śiva with the mantra consisting of the syllable "Ra" alone, and not otherwise.
Then, having fasted for a day and night, one should perform the recitation (japa) there.
"Rudra appears in person and grants whatever boon is desired.
Such are the supernatural powers found in the Kadalī forest;
there, at the entrance, the opening to Padmāvatī's subterranean chamber is inscribed in letters.
One yojana to the east of the lake stands [the place];
having performed *vamana* and *recana*, the practitioner should enter there.
He should go as far as a hundred *dhanvantaras*; there he will find a mṛdaṅga drum.
Upon seeing him, the hero shall then properly play for Padmāvatī;
she will come and give him nectar, by drinking which one becomes immortal.
Thereafter, she indeed entreats him: "Come to my palace."
"Accept five hundred divine maidens as your retinue;
I shall become your wife for as long as Brahmā lives. At the end of that time, we shall go to the supreme abode; of this there is no doubt."
The deity Kadambeshvara is situated in the south-eastern direction;
his lordship over progeny is established by the Kadamba tree standing at the edge of the eastern pond.
Having collected its leaves, one should smear them with pungent oil (kaṭutaila), or else with oils from the seeds of that tree; the wise man should cook them over a fire of its wood.
All those [leaves] become fish; he should then place them in a copper vessel.
One should consume [the substance] with honey and clarified butter, excluding the neck, tail, and head;
at that very moment, one becomes perfected, equal to Rudra, and possessed of great strength.
Furthermore, there is a tree located at the river site in Kuṇḍaleśvara.
Success shall be attained through the sequential application as before; there is no doubt in this matter.
To the north of the god Kapoteśvara stands Puṣpagiri;
one should diligently perform its circumambulation three times.
Then, by ascending the head [of the image], a man shall attain the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).
To the northeast of that, situated at the door of the *chelikā*,
one should enter facing north at a distance of three bow-lengths.
There are stones shaped like mice;
one should collect them, grind them with buttermilk, and drink that alone. One will fall into a swoon, but the perfected one (siddha) rises up in an instant and shall live for three days of Brahmā.
That very [substance] shall effect the liquefaction and penetration (sparśavedha) of all metals;
having fasted for a day and night, one shall attain success in the presence of the deity.
To the south of the god Kapoteśvara are two deities.
In the middle of that, one should dig a pit knee-deep; taking those stones which resemble gorocana, one should grind them with honey and clarified butter.
By drinking that, a mortal becomes long-lived for a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
To the northwest of the deity Kapoteśvara, one should dig a pit measuring one cubit; there lie stones resembling pigeons that pierce through touch.
Having performed the propitiation of the deity, one should cause one of them to be taken.
To the northeast of the deity Mallikārjuna, there exists the Bhṛgupātana;
near that is a pool from which one should take earth,
mix it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and heat it over charcoal of the Khadira wood.
Then, iron that resembles a blue lotus should indeed fall [into the crucible];
one should then sprinkle it at the door of Ambikā seven times, repeatedly, with honey and clarified butter after it has been thoroughly heated. 131.
A man who holds that ball in his mouth becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
To the east of Bhṛgupāta, within a distance of more than one *krośa*,
there is a mountain famous by the name Acchataila.

To the west of that is the entrance to a cave; five bow-lengths within it, one sees a pool whose liquid has the luster of lac. Having collected it in a gourd vessel, it becomes a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhī).
To the east of the god Mallikārjuna, there exists the world-renowned enclosure wall of Candragupta, and therein is his temple.
To the east of that stands a caitya, and to the east of the caitya is a great stone slab.
It is known as being the color of mung beans, and it possesses the power of transmuting through touch.
An elephant is also renowned to be there; having mounted it with a concentrated mind, one should take a blade of grass from its back, and all of that shall become gold.
On the northern side of the elephant, one should dig the earth to the depth of a knee;
there are those [substances] shaped like jambū fruits which possess the power of tactile transmutation.
Or else, one should dig beneath the elephant to the depth of a knee, and from that one shall obtain them.
The perfected triangular pill (guṭikā), which pierces a hundred thousand targets, is supreme.
To the northwest of Śrīśaila stands the Devahrada Tīrtha;
there, in the pool, are stones the color of mung beans that possess the power of touch-piercing.
There, the supreme *liṅga* resembling a tortoise, which effects the piercing of touch,
should be worshipped after performing the ritual on the full moon day of the month of Kṛttikā.
Two *gavyūtis* from there is what is known by the name Nīlavana.
There, the *liṅga* is blue in color and the water is likewise;

there are stones resembling horses, mangoes, and crows that possess the power of touch-transmutation (*sparśavedhaka*). One should dig within the temple until reaching the depth of a knee and then extract them.
To the southwest of Śrīśaila stands the one named Guṇḍiprabhā; from its summit, earth from a hollow should be taken—yellow in color—and one should burn it in crucibles.
From that, gold of shimmering form emerges, without a doubt.
In that very place, bees shall appear as before, bestowing their fruits.
Likewise, at the vast and auspicious holy site named Tambīpura, which is renowned for its eternal fruit, the wise man should practice as previously described. || 145-146 ||
One should go by the royal road to the place named Mahānandeśvara on the southwest side of Śrīśaila, on its northeastern flank;
there is the deity named Kālavarṇeśvara and his foremost sacrificial pool.
In its center there exists a liquid resembling an indragopaka insect.
By sprinkling it upon the seven heated metals, they become gold.
To the northeast of Śrīśaila is the deity Turaleśvara. || 148-149 ||
To the north of that is the most famous and excellent Umā-parvata;
upon its summit stand beautiful *darbha* grasses with the luster of tridents.
Having dug down to the depth of a hip beneath it, one should take away the blue clay.
One should cook that [food] with wood produced from trees other than the akṣa; one should set aside a portion for the gods, likewise a portion for the guest, and a portion for the fire.
One should eat the portion for oneself; such a man shall live for ten thousand kalpas.
There, near Iḷeśvara, is the famous Koṭīśvara; merely by touching a flower before it, one becomes a *sparśavedhin*.
Acaleśa is also located right there, the supreme bestower of *sparśavedha*.
One yojana to the south of Acaleśa,
there exists the deity named Amareśvara; on its auspicious golden stone slab,
one should place either beef or "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa).
Having kindled a fire with *badarī* wood, at dawn that cloth fragment, perfumed by the menses of women, appears like gold;
one should stir it with a stone and preserve it in a gourd vessel.
By merely touching it with that, iron becomes gold.
On Śrīśaila, right there, stones exist in the form of lumps;
one should always consume one karṣa of their powder together with Triphalā.
Indeed, by using it for half a month, one destroys old age and may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
To the southwest of the king of mountains is the lord Paṭāhakarṇa;
and in the northeastern direction from him, at a distance of twenty-five bow-lengths, [is another].
One should dig two cubits deep into a stone slab measuring two cubits in height; from there,
one should retrieve thirty stones resembling the hollows of *śrāva* flowers, heat them until they are red-hot like fire, and then drench them with the juices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* plants.
From the midst of that [curd], one should take the butter and offer a portion to the deity;
one portion should be given to the guest, and the wise man should consume one portion himself.
By this, fainting may occur for a day and night, after which the man becomes fully awakened.
That hero shall live for ten thousand years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
The second flight of stairs belonging to that deity effects touch-activation (sparśavedha).
Beside that deity, there are stones that are white and yellow.
Without doubt, one should collect all those [substances] that possess the power of touch;
to the east of that deity, there shall be a well not very far away.
In its center, there are stones resembling frogs which possess the power of touch-transfixion.
To the north of that deity is the famous Liṅgaparvata. On its northern side there is a river flowing toward the east;
on the western bank of that river is a liṅga of a tawny color.
There, a pool filled with mountain water shall exist, capable of piercing [the spiritual knots] in an instant.
Two yojanas to the south of Maheśa is Caṇḍikā, renowned as Piṇḍādevī; [she is located] from her northwestern corner.
A well stands in its center, and within it are stones the color of mung beans (169).
Likewise, there are others resembling myrobalan fruits; all of them possess the power of penetration through touch.
Herein, the method for penetrating all of them by means of touch is prescribed. (170)
If it is coarse, one should grind it finely and with that [powder] have a crucible (mūṣā) made;
within that, one should cause the eight metals to be transmuted.
All that becomes gold; thus one should act according to one's desire.
If there is even a minute amount of any of the eight molten metals anywhere,
one should cast it all into the middle [of the crucible], and it will all become gold.
To the northwest of Mallikārjuna is situated the Sarveśvara Tīrtha.
Having traveled half a yojana along the waterway in the southern direction from there, one sees a ḍāṅgarika tree;
on its top there are black emblic myrobalan fruits (dhātrīphala), which one should eat.
If practiced as desired for seven days, a man shall possess a vajra-body;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, he shall live for three hundred kalpas.
Furthermore, to the south of that is the great forest of Kākalerī.
There stands a plantain pillar; the practitioner should enter there and go for half a krośa, where a pool of mercury (rasakuṇḍa) is seen.
Taking [the mercury] in a bottle-gourd vessel, the mercury becomes "ten-million-fold piercing" (koṭivedhin).
In that forest, there shall be a peacock made of blue-colored stone. At its mouth is a pool, twelve finger-breadths deep and blue;
by casting a dry bamboo stalk into its center, it shall become fresh in an instant.
On that day, leaves, fruits, and flowers grow [from it], and not otherwise;
having thrown one *prastha* of mercury (*pārada*) there, one should then take away the water.
One should drink that [mixture] equal in measure to honey, and at that very moment, one will become unconscious.
Within a moment one shall obtain a kingdom and live for a thousand yugas.
On the south-eastern side of the mountain, there exists Siddhakeśvara, the Lord of the Magic Pill;
in front of him, one should dig five cubits into the earth.

There are stones shaped like jujube fruits that grant the power of moving through the sky; having collected even one of these and holding it in the mouth, those who travel through the air [attain their goal].
On Śrīśaila, the procedure for all the aforementioned yogas is now declared.
Having first performed the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*), one should subsequently recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
by that, one will swiftly attain the respective siddhis.
One should then invoke the deity of the sacred field (*kṣetradevatā*).
In that regard, a deity manifests in a dream and grants a boon;

thus, the practice of Śrīgiri-sādhana must be performed by those devoted to the mantra, who are most steadfast, faithful, and intent on the worship of Śambhu, who daily observe the rules of ritual, who are dedicated to recitation, and who have mastered the traditional scriptures. Otherwise, alas, it will certainly become a source of hardship, rejected and rendered utterly futile.

Thus ends the eighth instruction, titled "The Practice of Śrīparvata," in the Section on Alchemy (*Rasāyana-khaṇḍa*) of the *Rasaratnākara* composed by the Siddha Śrī Nityanātha, son of the venerable Pārvatī;
this Section on Alchemy is now complete.
The Śrīśaila mountain, however, is located in the Karṇāṭaka region of South India.
